title: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā
summary: The oldest Vedic collection: hymns (sūktas) of praise and invocation to Agni, Indra, Soma, Varuṇa, Mitra, the Aśvins, Uṣas, Rudra, Viṣṇu and others, recited by the hotṛ priest. Beside the liturgy it contains speculative hymns on the One (1.164, 10.129, 10.121, 10.90, 10.125), on speech, on the self and on death and the fathers (10.14–18).

attribution.tradition: authorless (apauruṣeya) revelation seen by the ṛṣis; arranged by Vyāsa; each hymn's seer (ṛṣi), deity and metre are recorded by the Anukramaṇīs
attribution.scholarly: composed by priestly poet families over several centuries and redacted into the Śākala recension

tradition.text: beginningless; the hymns were 'seen' by the ṛṣis and handed down (Nirukta 1.20)

scholarly.text: c. 1500–1000 BCE; family books (2–7) earliest, books 1 and 10 latest

structure.description: 10 maṇḍalas; 1,028 sūktas counting the 11 Vālakhilya hymns (8.49–59); c. 10,550 verses (counts differ slightly). Books 2–7 are the family books: 2 Gṛtsamada, 3 Viśvāmitra, 4 Vāmadeva, 5 Atri, 6 Bharadvāja, 7 Vasiṣṭha; book 8 chiefly the Kāṇvas (and Āṅgirasas); book 9 the hymns to Soma Pavamāna gathered from all families; books 1 and 10 are collections of many seers and are regarded as later. A second division into 8 aṣṭakas × 8 adhyāyas (64 adhyāyas) and vargas is used for recitation.

editions.name: F. Max Müller, Rig-Veda-Sanhita with the commentary of Sāyaṇa (London 1849–1874; 2nd ed. 1890–92)
Th. Aufrecht, Die Hymnen des Rigveda (Berlin 1861–63; transliterated)
Vaidika Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala, Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā with Sāyaṇa's commentary (Poona 1933–51)
B. van Nooten & G. Holland, Rig Veda: a metrically restored text (1994)
R. T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda (1889–92)
K. F. Geldner, Der Rig-Veda (1951)
S. W. Jamison & J. P. Brereton, The Rigveda (2014)

notes: Language: Vedic Sanskrit. The local copy used for spot-checks: sources_raw/DharmicData/Rigveda (Devanāgarī with accents, seer/deity/metre headers).

title: Ṛgveda Padapāṭha
summary: The word-by-word recitation of the Ṛgveda, ascribed to Śākalya, which undoes the euphonic combinations (sandhi) and marks compound members, so that every word and accent of the continuous text is fixed; it is the basis of the krama and other interwoven recitations and the oldest witness to how the tradition understood each word.

attribution.tradition: Śākalya
attribution.scholarly: the Padapāṭha is very old (pre-Pāṇinian); Śākalya is cited by Yāska and Pāṇini

scholarly.text: before Yāska and Pāṇini (c. 7th–5th c. BCE)

structure.description: follows the Saṃhitā hymn by hymn; omits a few verses it treats as not part of the Saṃhitā proper (e.g. 10.121.10 and the Vālakhilya hymns, as usually reported)

notes: The omission of 10.121.10 and of the Vālakhilya hymns from the Padapāṭha is recalled from secondary literature — confidence moderate.

title: Ṛgveda Khilāni (the supplementary hymns)
summary: A collection of supplementary hymns (khila) transmitted alongside the Śākala Saṃhitā — most fully in a Kashmiri manuscript — including the Śrī Sūkta, the Medhā Sūkta, the Śivasaṅkalpa verses and other hymns used in later worship.

attribution.tradition: part of the revealed hymns, not counted in the Saṃhitā
attribution.scholarly: later additions from the late Vedic period onward

structure.description: about 5 adhyāyas of khila hymns in the Kashmiri recension (as edited by Scheftelowitz, 1906)

notes: Division and contents recalled from memory; the Kashmiri manuscript edition (Scheftelowitz 1906) to be confirmed.

title: Śrī Sūkta
summary: A Ṛgveda khila hymn to Śrī-Lakṣmī, the goddess of fortune, invoked through Jātavedas (Agni); in later practice the principal Vedic hymn of Lakṣmī worship.
notes: Location 'Khila 2.6' from memory (low confidence).

title: Vālakhilya hymns
summary: Eleven hymns printed within book 8 (8.49–59) that the tradition treats as supplementary; they include the verse 'one Agni is kindled in many ways … one has become all this' (8.58.2).

title: Soma Pavamāna hymns (Ṛgveda book 9)
summary: The ninth maṇḍala: 114 hymns to Soma 'self-purifying' (pavamāna) as the juice flows through the woollen filter, gathered from all the priestly families. The book ends with Kaśyapa's prayer to be made immortal in the world of inexhaustible light (9.113); its own verses say that whoever studies these pāvamānī verses eats purified food (9.67.31).

title: Sāmaveda Saṃhitā (Kauthuma)
summary: The Veda of chants: verses (ṛc), nearly all taken from the Ṛgveda (mostly books 8 and 9), arranged as the texts (yoni) of melodies (sāman) sung by the udgātṛ priests at the soma sacrifice. The verse-books (ārcika) are the libretto; the melodies themselves are in the song-books (gāna). The tradition treats the Sāmaveda as the root of chant and of music.

attribution.tradition: authorless (apauruṣeya) revelation seen by the ṛṣis; arranged by Vyāsa; Jaimini received the Sāmaveda from Vyāsa (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.21)
attribution.scholarly: a liturgical anthology drawn largely from the Ṛgveda, arranged for the udgātṛ's chants

structure.description: Pūrvārcika (āgneya, aindra and pāvamāna parvans; then the Āraṇyaka section and the Mahānāmnī verses; c. 650 verses) and Uttarārcika (c. 1,225 verses in groups, mostly triplets); about 1,875 verses in the usual Kauthuma count (c. 1,800 in Griffith's edition), only some 75 not found in the Ṛgveda (counts differ).

editions.name: Th. Benfey, Die Hymnen des Sâma-Veda (1848)
Satyavrata Sāmaśramī, Sāmaveda-Saṃhitā with Sāyaṇa (Calcutta 1874–78)
R. T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Samaveda (1893)

notes: Verse counts from memory; the Pūrvārcika opens with 'agna ā yāhi vītaye' (= RV 6.16.10), as checked in the local Griffith dataset.

title: Jaiminīya Saṃhitā (Sāmaveda)
summary: The Sāmaveda Saṃhitā of the Jaiminīya (Talavakāra) school, with its own song-books; close to the Kauthuma in its verses but distinct in arrangement and melody.

attribution.tradition: the Sāmaveda as handed down by Jaimini's line
attribution.scholarly: a parallel Sāmaveda recension

editions.name: W. Caland, Die Jaiminīya-Saṃhitā (1907)

title: Grāmageya-gāna (Veyagāna)
summary: The first song-book of the Kauthuma–Rāṇāyanīya Sāmaveda: the melodies on the Pūrvārcika verses 'to be sung in the village', i.e. in public ritual; it shows how each verse is transformed into a sāman with stretched vowels, repetitions and stobhas.

title: Āraṇyageya-gāna (Araṇyegāna)
summary: The song-book of melodies 'to be sung in the forest', regarded as more powerful and secret, learned apart from the village; it includes the melodies of the Āraṇyaka section.

title: Ūha-gāna
summary: The song-book that applies the melodies to the Uttarārcika verse-groups in the order of the soma rites, 'modifying' (ūha) the base melodies for new texts.

title: Ūhya-gāna (Rahasya-gāna)
summary: The song-book applying the forest melodies to the ritual verse-groups; also called the 'secret' (rahasya) songs.

title: Nāradīya Śikṣā
summary: The phonetic manual of the Sāmaveda: it names the seven sāman notes and sets them against the notes of the flute (1.5.1–2: the first of the Sāman singers is the flute's madhyama, the second gāndhāra, the third ṛṣabha, the fourth ṣaḍja, the fifth dhaivata, the sixth niṣāda, the seventh pañcama), gives the places of the notes in the body and on the fingers (1.7), and teaches the gestures and faults of chanting.

attribution.tradition: Nārada
attribution.scholarly: a late Vedic / early post-Vedic śikṣā of the Sāmavedins

notes: Checked against sources_raw/raw_etexts/shixA/sAma-vedaH/naradiya_shiksha.md. Primary owner of śikṣā literature: U02.

title: Puṣpasūtra
summary: A Sāmaveda treatise on how verses are transformed into chants: the modifications (vikāra), insertions of stobhas and the distribution of melodies over the verses.

attribution.tradition: ascribed to Gobhila or to Vararuci (reports differ)
attribution.scholarly: late Vedic sūtra of the Sāmavedins

notes: Authorship reports recalled from memory; to be checked.

title: Taittirīya Saṃhitā
summary: The Black Yajurveda Saṃhitā of the Taittirīya school: the adhvaryu priest's formulas (yajus) and verses for the new- and full-moon rites, the soma sacrifice, the royal consecration, the building of the fire altar (agnicayana) and the horse sacrifice, interleaved with brāhmaṇa prose explaining them. Book 4 contains the Śatarudrīya (4.5) and the Camaka (4.7).

attribution.tradition: authorless (apauruṣeya) revelation seen by the ṛṣis; arranged by Vyāsa; handed down from Vaiśampāyana through his pupils, the Taittirīyas (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5)
attribution.scholarly: Black Yajurveda Saṃhitā, mantra and brāhmaṇa strata

scholarly.text: c. 1000–800 BCE (prose portions); mantras partly older

editions.name: A. Weber, Die Taittirîya-Saṃhitâ (1871–72)
A. B. Keith, The Veda of the Black Yajus School (1914)

title: Śatarudrīya (Śrī Rudram, Rudrādhyāya)
summary: The litany of homage to Rudra in his hundreds of forms: after asking Rudra to turn his wrath, bow and arrows away and to show his auspicious, non-terrible body (śivā tanūḥ aghorā), it pays homage (namaḥ) to Rudra as lord of paths, forests, hosts and animals, as present in thieves and craftsmen, in the small and the great, in waters, clouds and grass, and ends by placing the countless Rudras on earth far away. Its eighth section contains 'namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca', the source the Śaiva traditions give for the five-syllable formula.
notes: Used in the agnicayana to pacify Rudra; recited in the tradition as Rudra-japa (Ekādaśa-, Laghu-, Mahā-, Atirudra) and in Śaiva worship. The Jābāla Upaniṣad names śatarudrīya recitation as a means to immortality (reference only).

title: Camakam (Camaka-praśna)
summary: The Yajurveda litany that follows the Śatarudrīya: a long series of petitions 'and … for me' (… ca me) — food and impulse, the breaths, mind, speech, eye and ear, strength and life, truth and faith, well-being, the Vedic rites and their implements, and finally the numbers — each to be made fit by the sacrifice (yajñena kalpantām).
notes: Recited with the Śatarudrīya (Namakam-Camakam); ritually the formulas accompany the 'stream of wealth' (vasordhārā) offering of the agnicayana (moderate confidence).

title: Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā
summary: The Black Yajurveda Saṃhitā of the Maitrāyaṇīya school: mantras and brāhmaṇa prose for the śrauta rites, in four books; an important parallel to the Taittirīya and Kāṭhaka texts.

attribution.tradition: authorless (apauruṣeya) revelation seen by the ṛṣis; arranged by Vyāsa
attribution.scholarly: Black Yajurveda Saṃhitā

editions.name: L. von Schroeder, Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (1881–86)

title: Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā
summary: The Black Yajurveda Saṃhitā of the Kaṭha school: mantras and brāhmaṇa prose, closely parallel to the Maitrāyaṇī; preserved in Kashmiri manuscripts.

attribution.tradition: authorless (apauruṣeya) revelation seen by the ṛṣis; arranged by Vyāsa; the Kaṭhas descend from Kaṭha, pupil of Vaiśampāyana
attribution.scholarly: Black Yajurveda Saṃhitā

structure.description: 40 sthānakas plus appended sections (as usually counted)

editions.name: L. von Schroeder, Kâṭhakam: die Saṃhitâ der Kaṭha-Çâkhâ (1900–10)

notes: Structure count from memory (moderate-low).

title: Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha Saṃhitā
summary: The fragmentary Saṃhitā of the Kapiṣṭhala branch of the Kaṭhas, close to the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.

editions.name: Raghu Vira, Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha-Saṃhitā (1932)

title: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Mādhyandina)
summary: The White Yajurveda Saṃhitā: the adhvaryu's formulas and verses without explanatory prose (which is given separately in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa). Its forty adhyāyas run through the new- and full-moon rites, agnihotra and seasonal rites, the soma sacrifice, the royal rites, the fire altar (11–18, with the Śatarudrīya in 16), the sautrāmaṇī and the horse sacrifice (22–25), then supplementary books with the Puruṣa Sūkta (31), the hymn of the One (32), the Śivasaṅkalpa verses on mind (34.1–6), the funeral (35), peace chants (36) and the pravargya, and closes with the Īśa Upaniṣad (40).

attribution.tradition: Yājñavalkya received these Yajus, unknown to his teacher, from the Sun in the form of a horse (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.26–29)
attribution.scholarly: White Yajurveda Saṃhitā; adhyāyas 26–40 are supplementary (khila) layers

tradition.text: revealed to Yājñavalkya by the Sun

structure.description: 40 adhyāyas; c. 1,975 kaṇḍikās (Mādhyandina count, as usually given)

editions.name: A. Weber, The Vâjasaneyi-Sanhitâ in the Mâdhyandina and the Kâṇva-çâkhâ (1852)
R. T. H. Griffith, The Texts of the White Yajurveda (1899)

notes: Adhyāya 40 is the Īśa Upaniṣad (src:isa-upanisad, owned by U03). Wording of cited verses checked against sources_raw/DharmicData/Yajurveda.

title: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Kāṇva)
summary: The Kāṇva recension of the White Yajurveda Saṃhitā, parallel to the Mādhyandina with differences of order and wording; its last adhyāya is the Kāṇva form of the Īśa Upaniṣad.

attribution.tradition: Yājñavalkya's Yajus as transmitted by Kaṇva's line
attribution.scholarly: White Yajurveda recension

title: Śivasaṅkalpa Sūkta
summary: Six verses on the mind (manas), each ending 'may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve (śivasaṅkalpa)': the divine mind that goes far in waking and returns in sleep, the one light of lights; the inner immortal light in beings without which no act is done; the mind that holds past, present and future and in which the Vedas are set like spokes in a hub; the heart-seated charioteer that guides men like horses.
notes: A form of these verses also circulates among the Ṛgveda khilas (reference only).

title: Atharvaveda Saṃhitā (Śaunaka)
summary: The Veda of the Atharvans and Aṅgirases: hymns and spells for healing (bhaiṣajya), long life, protection against demons and sorcery, concord in family and assembly, marriage, royal power, expiation and prosperity; speculative hymns on Skambha the frame of the world (10.7–8), the human body as the city of the gods (10.2), Prāṇa (11.4), the Brahmacārin (11.5), the Remainder (11.7), the Earth (12.1), Time (19.53–54); the prose book of the Vrātya (15); the funeral book (18).

attribution.tradition: authorless (apauruṣeya) revelation seen by the ṛṣis; arranged by Vyāsa; the Atharvaveda was received by Sumantu (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.22)
attribution.scholarly: a collection of popular-ritual and speculative hymns, parts as old as the late Ṛgveda

scholarly.text: c. 1200–900 BCE for most hymns (low confidence)

structure.description: 20 kāṇḍas, c. 730 sūktas, c. 6,000 verses; books 1–7 short hymns grouped by length, 8–12 long hymns, 13 Rohita, 14 marriage, 15 Vrātya (prose), 16–17 protective formulas, 18 funeral, 19 supplement, 20 Indra hymns for the soma rite (mostly from the Ṛgveda, with the Kuntāpa hymns). Books 9.9–10 reproduce RV 1.164.

editions.name: R. Roth & W. D. Whitney, Atharva Veda Sanhita (1856)
W. D. Whitney (rev. C. R. Lanman), Atharva-Veda Saṃhitā (1905)
R. T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Atharvaveda (1895–96)

notes: Sūkta numbering in some printed editions (e.g. the local DharmicData text) splits book 13 into more sūktas than Whitney's four; refs here follow Whitney unless noted.

title: Atharvaveda Saṃhitā (Paippalāda)
summary: The second Atharvaveda recension, in twenty books, overlapping the Śaunaka in many hymns but with much material of its own; long known from a single Kashmiri birch-bark manuscript in Śāradā script and later from manuscripts and living reciters in Odisha.

attribution.tradition: the Atharvaveda as transmitted in Pippalāda's line
attribution.scholarly: a parallel Atharvaveda recension

editions.name: L. C. Barret, The Kashmirian Atharva Veda (1905–40)
Dipak Bhattacharya, Paippalāda-Saṃhitā of the Atharvaveda (Kolkata 1997–)

notes: Teachings from this recension are not recorded here (no verse-level recall); gap listed in REPORT.md.

title: The Vrātya book (Atharvaveda 15)
summary: A prose book on the Vrātya: a wandering, vow-bound figure who stirs Prajāpati into creation, becomes Mahādeva and Īśāna, takes up the rainbow bow, stands upright for a year, is given a seat made of the seasons and the Vedas, and is honoured as a cosmic guest; his seven prāṇas, apānas and vyānas are identified with fire, sun, moon, wind, waters, animals and creatures.

title: Skambha hymns (Atharvaveda 10.7–8)
summary: Two long hymns asking in which limb of Skambha, the 'frame' or 'pillar' of the world, tapas, ṛta, vrata, faith and truth abide; they identify Skambha with the highest Brahman (jyeṣṭha brahman) to whom homage is paid, teach that those who know Brahman in man know the Supreme, and end with the self, desireless, wise, immortal, self-born, knowing whom one does not fear death.

title: Kena Sūkta (Atharvaveda 10.2)
summary: The hymn on the making of man ('by whom were the heels of man set?'), attributed to Nārāyaṇa: it asks by whom the limbs, senses, mind, faith and speech were placed in him and answers 'by Brahman'; it names the body the eight-wheeled, nine-gated city of the gods with a golden sheath in which dwells the self-possessed wonder (yakṣa) known to the knowers of Brahman.

title: Prāṇa Sūkta (Atharvaveda 11.4)
summary: Homage to Prāṇa, the life-breath, lord of all, in whom all is established: Prāṇa clothes creatures as a father his dear son; it is death and fever; the gods revere it; it stays awake among sleepers; the swan rising from the waters never lifts one foot, else there would be no today or tomorrow; the speaker binds Prāṇa to himself for life.

title: Brahmacārin Sūkta (Atharvaveda 11.5)
summary: The hymn of the Vedic student: the brahmacārin moves quickening both worlds; the teacher, initiating him, holds him three nights as an embryo; with fuel, girdle, toil and tapas he fills the worlds; by brahmacarya and tapas the king protects the realm, a maiden wins a husband, the gods struck down death.

title: Ucchiṣṭa Sūkta (Atharvaveda 11.7)
summary: The hymn of the Remainder (ucchiṣṭa) of the sacrifice as the ground of all: in the Remainder are name and form (nāma-rūpa), the world, Indra and Agni, the rites, the Vedas and all beings.

title: Pṛthivī Sūkta (Atharvaveda 12.1)
summary: The sixty-three-verse hymn to the Earth: she is upheld by truth, great order, consecration, tapas, brahman and sacrifice; 'the Earth is mother, I am her son'; she bears peoples of many speeches and many dharmas; the digger asks that what he digs may grow again and that he not strike her vitals or heart.

title: Kāla Sūkta (Atharvaveda 19.53–54)
summary: Two hymns on Time (kāla) as the first god: the seven-reined, thousand-eyed horse whom the poets mount, whose wheels are all beings; in Time are tapas, the eldest and brahman; Time is lord of all and father of Prajāpati; from Time arose the waters, brahman, tapas and the quarters.

title: Kauśika Sūtra
summary: The ritual manual of the Śaunaka Atharvaveda that prescribes how its hymns are used in domestic, healing, protective, pacificatory and sorcery rites — with amulets, herbs, water and fire.

attribution.tradition: Kauśika
attribution.scholarly: late Vedic sūtra of the Śaunakīya Atharvavedins

notes: Primary owner of kalpa literature: U02; recorded here because it gives the viniyoga of the Atharvaveda healing hymns.

title: Atharvaveda Pariśiṣṭas
summary: Appendices of the Atharvaveda (traditionally seventy-two) on omens and portents, royal and pacificatory rites, and the Atharvavedic recitation tradition, including a Caraṇavyūha listing the śākhās.
notes: Number and contents recalled from memory; to be checked.

title: Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya
summary: The Śākala school's treatise on the phonetics of the Ṛgveda: sounds, accents, the rules for joining the words of the Padapāṭha into the continuous text, and the krama recitation.

attribution.tradition: Śaunaka
attribution.scholarly: late Vedic phonetic treatise of the Śākala school

notes: Primary owner of prātiśākhya literature: U02.

title: Sarvānukramaṇī
summary: Kātyāyana's index to the Ṛgveda, giving for every hymn its first words, number of verses, seer (ṛṣi), deity (devatā) and metre (chandas); the traditional source of the seer attributions recorded in this ontology.

attribution.tradition: Kātyāyana
attribution.scholarly: late Vedic index building on Śaunaka's anukramaṇīs

title: Bṛhaddevatā
summary: Śaunaka's metrical treatise on the deities of the Ṛgveda hymns, hymn by hymn, with the legends (itihāsa) behind them; it lists the women seers (brahmavādinī) of the Ṛgveda and discusses how the one Ātman is praised under many deities.

attribution.tradition: Śaunaka
attribution.scholarly: late Vedic–early classical compilation; date debated

title: Caraṇavyūha
summary: A short treatise listing the branches (śākhās, caraṇas) of the four Vedas and their extent — e.g. the five Ṛgveda śākhās (Śākala, Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, Māṇḍūkāyana) — ascribed to Śaunaka or Kātyāyana; the Atharvaveda has its own Caraṇavyūha among its Pariśiṣṭas.

attribution.tradition: Śaunaka (or Kātyāyana)
attribution.scholarly: late compilation; its counts of śākhās are traditional

notes: Ascription and exact lists recalled from memory; to be checked.

title: Ṛgvidhāna
summary: A manual on the uses (vidhāna) of Ṛgveda hymns and verses for purification, expiation, healing and the fulfilment of wishes by recitation (japa) and oblation, ascribed to Śaunaka.

title: Vikṛtivallī
summary: A short treatise defining the eight 'modified' recitations (vikṛti) of the Veda built on the krama — jaṭā, mālā, śikhā, rekhā, dhvaja, daṇḍa, ratha and ghana.
notes: Ascription to Vyāḍi and the verse listing the eight vikṛtis are recalled from memory — low confidence.

title: Pāṇinīya Śikṣā
summary: The general phonetic manual ascribed to Pāṇini: places and efforts of articulation, the Vedic accents and the conduct of recitation — naming six worst and six best reciters (32–33) and warning that a mantra wrong in accent or letter becomes a verbal thunderbolt that harms the sacrificer, as 'Indra-śatru' did through a fault of accent (52).

attribution.tradition: Pāṇini
attribution.scholarly: a later śikṣā in Pāṇini's name

notes: Verse numbers checked against sources_raw/raw_etexts/shixA/sAdhAraNI/paniniya_shiksha.md. Primary owner: U02.

title: Asya Vāmasya Sūkta (the riddle hymn, Ṛgveda 1.164)
summary: Dīrghatamas' hymn of riddles (brahmodya): the one-wheeled chariot of seven names; the twelve-spoked wheel of ṛta with its 720 sons; the two birds on one tree, one eating the sweet fig, the other looking on; the seer who does not know what he is until the first-born of ṛta comes to him; the immortal of one origin with the mortal; the syllable in the highest heaven on which the gods sit; the four quarters of speech, three hidden; and the one Being that the inspired call by many names.

attribution.tradition: seen by dirghatamas; deity: the All-gods (Viśvedevāḥ) and others (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Reproduced in the Atharvaveda (Śaunaka 9.9–10). An adhyātma (inner) commentary on this hymn by one Ātmānanda is reported in the secondary literature (low confidence; not entered as a source).

title: Nāsadīya Sūkta (the creation hymn, Ṛgveda 10.129)
summary: The hymn of the beginning: then there was neither non-being nor being, neither death nor immortality; That One breathed, windless, by its own power; darkness hidden by darkness; That One was born by the power of heat (tapas); desire, the first seed of mind, arose; seers searching in the heart found the bond of being in non-being; the gods came later than this creation, so who knows whence it came — he who oversees it in the highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps he does not know.

attribution.tradition: seen by prajapati-paramesthin; deity: bhāvavṛtta (the course of becoming) (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Recited also in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (2.8.9, reference from memory).

title: Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90)
summary: The hymn of the cosmic Person: thousand-headed, thousand-eyed, thousand-footed, covering the earth and exceeding it by ten fingers; all this is Puruṣa, past and future; one quarter of him is all beings, three quarters the immortal in heaven; from him Virāj was born and from Virāj he; the gods sacrificed Puruṣa as the oblation, and from that sacrifice came the verses, chants, metres and formulas, the animals, the four varṇas from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet, the moon from his mind, the sun from his eye, Indra and Agni from his mouth, wind from his breath, and the worlds; 'with the sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; these were the first dharmas'.

attribution.tradition: seen by narayana-rsi; deity: Puruṣa (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Also Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 31.1–16 (with the six 'Uttaranārāyaṇa' verses 31.17–22), Atharvaveda (Śaunaka) 19.6 and Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12 (last two from memory). Its sixteen verses are used for the sixteen-fold worship in later temple and domestic ritual.

title: Hiraṇyagarbha Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.121)
summary: The hymn with the refrain 'to which god shall we offer with oblation?' (kasmai devāya haviṣā vidhema): the Golden Germ arose in the beginning, born the one lord of what exists; he holds earth and heaven; he gives self and strength; his shadow is immortality and death; the great waters bearing the germ brought forth Agni, and from them arose the one life-breath of the gods; the last verse names him Prajāpati.

attribution.tradition: seen by hiranyagarbha-prajapatya; deity: Ka (Prajāpati) (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: The tradition reads the interrogative 'ka' (who?) as a name of Prajāpati. Verse 10 is widely held to be a later addition and is omitted in the Padapāṭha (as usually reported). Also VS 23.1 and TS 4.1.8 (checked).

title: Vāk Sūkta (Devī Sūkta, Ṛgveda 10.125)
summary: Speech (Vāc) proclaims herself: she moves with the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas and All-gods and bears Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra-Agni and the Aśvins; she is the queen, the gatherer of treasures, first of those worthy of worship, placed by the gods in many places; through her one eats, sees, breathes and hears, and those who do not know her dwell beside her; whom she loves she makes formidable, a brahman, a seer, a sage; she bends Rudra's bow; she gives birth to the father on the world's head; her womb is in the waters; she blows forth like the wind, beyond heaven and earth.

attribution.tradition: seen by vak-ambhrni; deity: Ātmā (the self) (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: The Sarvānukramaṇī gives the deity as 'ātman': the seer Vāc Āmbhṛṇī praises herself as the self of all. Recited in Śākta worship with the Devī Māhātmya.

title: Keśi Sūkta (the long-haired sage, Ṛgveda 10.136)
summary: The hymn of the long-haired one (keśin) who bears fire, poison(-drink) and heaven and earth, who is called this light; of the wind-girdled silent sages (munis) clad in soiled brown, who follow the wind's course when the gods enter them; 'ecstatic with munihood we have mounted the winds — you mortals see only our bodies'; the muni flies through the air seeing all forms, dwells by both oceans, knows the minds of apsarases, gandharvas and beasts, and drank from the cup with Rudra.

attribution.tradition: seen by vatarasana-munis; deity: the Keśins (Agni, Sūrya, Vāyu) (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Each verse is ascribed to one of seven wind-girdled munis: Jūti, Vātajūti, Viprajūti, Vṛṣāṇaka, Karikrata, Etaśa, Ṛśyaśṛṅga (checked in the local text's header).

title: Jñāna Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.71)
summary: Bṛhaspati's hymn on sacred speech and knowledge: the first speech arose when the ancients gave names; the wise fashioned speech with mind, sifting it like grain in a sieve; by sacrifice they followed speech's track and found her entered into the seers; one who sees does not see her, one who hears does not hear her, but to another she opens herself like a loving wife; knowing the words without their meaning is fruitless.

attribution.tradition: seen by brhaspati-angirasa; deity: jñāna (knowledge) (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

title: Viśvakarma Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.81–82)
summary: Two hymns to Viśvakarman, the All-maker: the seer-priest who offered all these worlds; with eyes, faces, arms and feet on every side he forged heaven and earth; what was the wood, what the tree from which they were fashioned?; he is our father, the disposer, the one name-giver of the gods; you will not find him who made these things — something else stands between you — and the hymn-reciters wander wrapped in mist and chatter.

attribution.tradition: seen by visvakarman-bhauvana; deity: Viśvakarman (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

title: Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.190)
summary: The three 'sin-effacing' verses: ṛta and satya were born from kindled tapas; then night, then the ocean; from the ocean the year, which orders days and nights; the Disposer fashioned sun and moon as before (yathāpūrvam), and heaven, earth, atmosphere and the light.

attribution.tradition: seen by aghamarsana; deity: bhāvavṛtta (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Recited while immersed in water at the bath and in the twilight worship (sandhyā) to efface sin.

title: The funeral hymns (Ṛgveda 10.14–18)
summary: The hymns for the dead: homage to Yama, first of mortals to find the path to the fathers (10.14); invocation of the fathers (10.15); the cremation fire asked not to consume the body utterly but to carry the dead, cooked, to the fathers, eye to the sun, breath to the wind (10.16); Pūṣan as guide on the far paths (10.17); death sent away on its own path, the living set apart by a boundary, the widow bidden to rise to the world of the living, and the bones laid in mother earth (10.18).

attribution.tradition: seen by yama-vaivasvata (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Seers per the Anukramaṇī: 10.14 Yama Vaivasvata; 10.15 Śaṅkha Yāmāyana; 10.16 Damana Yāmāyana; 10.17 Devaśravas Yāmāyana; 10.18 Saṅkusuka Yāmāyana (checked in the local text).

title: Gāyatrī (Sāvitrī) mantra (Ṛgveda 3.62.10)
summary: The verse to Savitṛ in the gāyatrī metre: 'we meditate on that excellent radiance of the god Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts (dhī)'. Prefixed with Oṃ and the three vyāhṛtis (bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ) as in VS 36.3, it is the mantra given at initiation (upanayana) and repeated in the twilight worship; the tradition calls it the mother of the Vedas.

attribution.tradition: seen by visvamitra; deity: Savitṛ (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Also TS 1.5.6 and 4.1.11 and VS 3.35, 22.9, 30.2, 36.3 (TS and VS 36.3 checked; the rest from memory).

title: Mahāmṛtyuñjaya (Tryambaka) mantra (Ṛgveda 7.59.12)
summary: The verse to the three-eyed (or three-mothered) one, Tryambaka: 'we worship Tryambaka, fragrant, increaser of prosperity; like a cucumber from its stalk, may I be freed from death, not from immortality'. The Anukramaṇī gives its deity as Rudra and calls it the verse that releases from death (mṛtyu-vimocanī).

attribution.tradition: seen by vasistha; deity: Rudra (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Also TS 1.8.6.2 and VS 3.60 (both checked); VS 3.60 adds a second form for maidens ('pativedanam … ito mukṣīya māmutaḥ'); the Atharvaveda marriage book has a parallel addressed to Aryaman (AVŚ 14.1.17).

title: Śraddhā Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.151)
summary: Faith (śraddhā) invoked: by faith the fire is kindled and the oblation offered; faith is honoured at morning, noon and sunset; 'Faith, make us faithful here'.

attribution.tradition: seen by sraddha-kamayani; deity: Śraddhā (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

title: Rātri Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.127)
summary: Night as a goddess who looks out with many eyes, fills the wide space, drives away darkness with her light, and gives rest to villages, beasts and birds; she is asked to ward off wolf and thief.

attribution.tradition: seen by ratri-bharadvaji; deity: Rātri (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

notes: Seer given as Kuśika Saubhara or Rātri Bhāradvājī (checked in the local text's header). A separate Rātri Sūkta is recited with the Devī Māhātmya (reference only).

title: Saṃjñāna Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.191)
summary: The last hymn of the Ṛgveda, on concord: 'go together, speak together, let your minds know together'; common be your counsel, assembly, mind and intention.

attribution.tradition: seen by samvanana-angirasa; deity: saṃjñāna (concord) (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

title: Akṣa Sūkta (the gambler's hymn, Ṛgveda 10.34)
summary: The gambler's lament: the dice ruin home, wife and mother, yet he cannot keep from them; the god Savitṛ tells him 'do not play with dice — till your field and delight in wealth'.

attribution.tradition: seen by kavasa-ailusa; deity: the dice; the gambler's reproach (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

title: Oṣadhi Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.97)
summary: The physician's hymn to the healing plants, born three ages before the gods; where plants gather like kings in assembly, that inspired one is called a physician, slayer of demons and dispeller of disease.

attribution.tradition: seen by bhisag-atharvana; deity: the plants (oṣadhayaḥ) (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

title: Sāyaṇa's commentary on the Ṛgveda (Vedārthaprakāśa)
summary: The complete classical commentary on the Ṛgveda, produced at Vijayanagara under Sāyaṇa's direction: it glosses every word, explains each hymn chiefly by its use in the sacrifice (yajña), draws on Yāska, the Brāhmaṇas and earlier commentators, and in its introduction defines the Veda and defends its authority. Most traditional and modern readings of the Ṛgveda start from it.

attribution.tradition: Sāyaṇa (the commentaries are also called 'Mādhavīya', after his brother Mādhava)
attribution.scholarly: composed by Sāyaṇa with collaborators, 14th century

editions.name: F. Max Müller (1849–74)
Vaidika Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala, Poona (1933–51)

notes: Sāyaṇa also commented on the Taittirīya, Sāma and Atharva Saṃhitās and on Brāhmaṇas and Āraṇyakas.

title: Sāyaṇa's commentary on the Taittirīya Saṃhitā
summary: Sāyaṇa's commentary on the Black Yajurveda Saṃhitā, whose introduction sets out why the Yajurveda, as the Veda of the adhvaryu who performs the rite, is commented on first.
notes: The reason given for commenting on the Yajurveda first is recalled from memory (moderate-low).

title: Sāyaṇa's commentary on the Atharvaveda
summary: Sāyaṇa's commentary on the Śaunaka Atharvaveda, surviving for most but not all of its books.
notes: Which books lack the commentary is not recalled with confidence.

title: Skandasvāmin's commentary on the Ṛgveda
summary: An early surviving Ṛgveda commentary, covering part of the Saṃhitā, which explains words through Yāska's etymologies and the ritual.
notes: Tradition reports that Skandasvāmin worked with Nārāyaṇa and Udgītha on the whole Ṛgveda; only parts survive (low confidence).

title: Ṛgarthadīpikā (Veṅkaṭamādhava)
summary: A concise commentary on the whole Ṛgveda by Veṅkaṭamādhava, giving brief glosses and the sense of each verse.

title: Jñānayajña (Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara on the Taittirīya Saṃhitā)
summary: Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara Miśra's commentary on the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (and Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka), older than Sāyaṇa's and often cited for its accentual and ritual explanations.

title: Mantrabhāṣya (Uvaṭa on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā)
summary: Uvaṭa's commentary on the Mādhyandina Saṃhitā, composed (by his own report) at Avantī under King Bhoja; Uvaṭa also commented on the Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya.

title: Vedadīpa (Mahīdhara on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā)
summary: Mahīdhara's commentary on the Mādhyandina Saṃhitā, composed at Vārāṇasī, the standard later commentary of the White Yajurveda, largely following Uvaṭa.

title: Ṛgbhāṣya (Madhva on Ṛgveda 1.1–40)
summary: Madhva's commentary on the first forty hymns of the Ṛgveda, which reads the hymns as ultimately praising Viṣṇu, the one denoted by all names, and holds that the mantras carry several levels of meaning.
notes: Commented on by Jayatīrtha and Rāghavendra (reference from memory). The 'three meanings' doctrine is recalled with moderate confidence.

title: Ṛgvedādibhāṣyabhūmikā (Dayānanda Sarasvatī)
summary: Dayānanda Sarasvatī's introduction to his Veda commentaries: the four Saṃhitās alone are the eternal revelation of one God; the names Agni, Indra and the rest denote that one God; the Vedas contain no history of persons; their knowledge is open to all.
notes: Recent (post-1800). Dates recalled with moderate confidence.

title: The Secret of the Veda (Sri Aurobindo)
summary: Sri Aurobindo's reading of the Ṛgveda as a symbolic record of inner experience: Agni as the divine will, Soma as delight, the cows as rays of light and knowledge, ṛta as the truth-consciousness.
notes: Recent (post-1800); an interpretation from outside the recitation lineages, recorded as such.
